paragraphs: Adversarial reprogramming changes a network’s inputs so that it performs a different task while its weights remain fixed. This paper revisits whether that ability requires a trained network. Its central finding is that random weights can already support reliable reprogramming under specified theoretical conditions and experimental initialization choices.

The authors prove a result for two-layer networks with ReLU activations and random weights. On Bernoulli data models defined over the vertices of a hypercube, these networks can be reprogrammed to achieve arbitrarily high accuracy, provided their width does not exceed their input dimension. The guarantee concerns this particular network and data setting.

The paper also strengthens a theoretical result about the direction taken by gradient-flow training. A consequence is that training on orthogonally separable datasets can cause reprogramming to fail. Supporting experiments show that untrained networks are susceptible when batch-normalization layers are suitably initialized. Together, these findings challenge the idea that prior training is required and show that training can sometimes reduce reprogrammability.
neurips-2022-adversarial-reprogramming-r.tldr: Random networks can support adversarial reprogramming under specific conditions, while training can sometimes make it fail.

paragraphs: An assistive system can help someone complete a task without helping them learn to do it independently. This paper focuses on that distinction for motor control: activities in which people must coordinate actions over time. The objective is to teach the human skills needed for eventual self-control, accounting for their ability to improve.

The proposed teaching algorithm uses skill-discovery methods from reinforcement learning to divide motor tasks into teachable components. It then builds practice drills from these skills and individualizes the curriculum for students with different capabilities. This makes the structure of practice part of the teaching method, rather than requiring every student to rehearse complete task trajectories.

The authors evaluate the approach through synthetic and human-user studies involving joystick-controlled car parking and writing Balinese characters. Skill-based assisted teaching improves student performance by around 40% relative to practicing full trajectories without skills. Individualized drills can provide up to 25% further improvement. These results support teaching smaller skills and adapting practice in the studied tasks.
neurips-2022-assistive-teaching-of-motor.tldr: Breaking motor tasks into teachable skills and personalizing practice drills improved human learning in two studied tasks.

paragraphs: A neural network’s performance can depend strongly on its hyperparameters, so finding a good configuration often requires repeated training runs. Even sophisticated search methods can be expensive when each candidate is trained using the entire dataset. AUTOMATA addresses the cost of these individual trials by reducing the data used during tuning.

The method selects informative subsets using gradient information. Its central idea is that a carefully chosen portion of the training data can provide enough guidance to identify useful hyperparameter settings more quickly. The selected subset therefore serves the tuning process: the question is whether configurations found with less training data deliver performance comparable to configurations found using all the data.

Experiments cover real-world datasets in text, vision, and tabular domains. The authors report tuning speedups ranging from 3× to 30×, with comparable performance from the resulting hyperparameters. These empirical findings suggest that dataset selection can substantially reduce tuning turnaround time while preserving the practical value of the search in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-automata-gradient-based-dat.tldr: AUTOMATA uses gradient-selected data subsets to speed up hyperparameter tuning while retaining comparable resulting performance.

paragraphs: Recovering an animal’s three-dimensional shape and movable skeleton from a single-camera video requires understanding how its parts connect and move. The paper argues that optimizing individual bone transformations without considering their connections can produce poor shape and articulation. CASA instead begins with an existing articulated character that provides useful structural information.

Its first stage searches a bank of three-dimensional character assets. A pretrained image-language model scores how well rendered views of candidate characters match the input video. The retrieved character then enters a neural inverse-graphics framework, which works backward from observed images to estimate the underlying animated model.

Within this framework, CASA jointly optimizes shape deformation, skeletal structure, and skinning weights—the quantities that determine how the surface follows the skeleton. This couples appearance and articulation instead of treating bone movements independently. Experiments support the method’s effectiveness for shape reconstruction and articulation, and the authors demonstrate re-animation of the reconstructed character. The output can therefore serve as a movable character, beyond representing the observed shape.
neurips-2022-casa-category-agnostic-skel.tldr: CASA retrieves an articulated character and jointly adapts its shape and skeleton to reconstruct a re-animatable animal from video.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning trains a network to represent examples in a space where their relationships can be compared. A central difficulty is that evaluation uses classes absent from training. Coded residual transform, or CRT, aims to make these learned representations transfer more effectively to those new classes.

CRT learns diverse prototype features and projects a feature map onto each prototype. It represents the features through the residual differences from these projections, weighted by their correlations with the prototypes. Each prototype supplies another perspective, so the representation captures relative differences across multiple reference points. The method also encourages consistency between feature-similarity matrices produced with different prototype counts and embedding dimensions.

Analyses of embedding-space density and spectral decay support the claimed improvement in generalization. Experiments and ablations report substantial gains over existing deep metric learning methods, including an improvement of up to 4.28% over the current best method on CUB. The findings support residual-based, multi-perspective encoding as a way to improve transfer to unseen classes in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2022-coded-residual-transform-fo.tldr: CRT improves metric-learning generalization by encoding features as weighted differences from multiple learned prototypes.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to adapt as data arrives from different environments while retaining performance on earlier ones. These two demands can conflict: learning the current environment may erase useful earlier behavior. This paper gives a theoretical framework for expressing both goals through feature extraction.

In the framework, learning each environment updates both a feature representation and a classifier. For linear features, the authors introduce DPGrad, an efficient gradient-based algorithm. Within their formalization, it comes with guarantees for performing well in the current environment while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. The contribution is therefore a defined learning setup together with an algorithm that satisfies its requirements.

The nonlinear case exposes a fundamental obstruction. For the general setting with nonlinear features, the authors show that an algorithm providing the same guarantees cannot exist, even without a computational-efficiency requirement. This separates an efficiently solvable linear case from a general impossibility result. The distinction concerns the paper’s formal guarantees; it does not claim that every practical use of nonlinear continual learning must fail.
neurips-2022-continual-learning-a-featur.tldr: A feature-extraction framework yields a guaranteed continual-learning algorithm for linear features and an impossibility result for the general nonlinear case.

paragraphs: A threshold policy chooses an action by checking whether one part of a system’s state exceeds a boundary determined by other state components. This paper studies how to learn the optimal policy of that form. Its central idea is to use the policy’s monotone structure directly in the learning algorithm.

The authors prove that this structure gives the policy gradient a particularly simple expression. They use that expression to construct an off-policy actor-critic algorithm for learning threshold policies. Simulations show substantial improvements over other reinforcement-learning algorithms, which the authors attribute to exploiting monotonicity. The result connects a structural property of the decision rule to a more effective learning procedure.

The paper also connects threshold-policy learning to restless multi-armed bandits through the Whittle index. It shows that finding this index is equivalent to finding an optimal threshold policy for an alternative problem. This leads to an index-learning algorithm using the same basic approach. In simulations, it learns the index much faster than several recent methods that estimate it indirectly.
neurips-2022-deeptop-deep-threshold-opti.tldr: DeepTOP exploits threshold-policy structure to simplify policy gradients and accelerate control-policy and Whittle-index learning in simulations.

paragraphs: SMRL is a model-based reinforcement-learning algorithm for episodes of fixed finite length. It studies environments whose transition distributions belong to an exponential family described by d parameters. The reward is assumed to be bounded and known, so the learning problem centers on the unknown transition model.

The algorithm estimates that model with score matching, a density-estimation technique that can work with unnormalized distributions. In this setting, score matching makes parameter estimation possible through ridge regression. SMRL combines this estimation procedure with an optimistic approach to decision-making, providing a connection between a tractable statistical estimation method and an online learning guarantee.

Under standard regularity assumptions, the authors bound online regret at roughly d times the square root of H cubed times T, where H is episode length and T is total interactions. The stated rate suppresses logarithmic factors and polynomial dependence on structural scale parameters. Its significance is a quantitative bound on accumulated learning cost in the specified model class, with explicit dependence on parameter count, episode length, and experience.
neurips-2022-exponential-family-model-ba.tldr: SMRL uses score matching to estimate exponential-family transition models efficiently and obtain a conditional online-regret guarantee.

paragraphs: Compressing a large language model often involves manually choosing a smaller student architecture and trying several alternatives. A different computational budget can require repeating that process. AutoDistil uses neural architecture search to produce students at multiple costs while addressing interference between differently sized subnetworks that share training weights.

The framework partitions the Transformer architecture search space into several compact regions using inductive biases and heuristics. Each region gets its own SuperLM, whose candidate students share weights. Training uses a task-agnostic objective, such as distilling self-attention, rather than requiring labels for a particular downstream task. A lightweight search then selects a student without retraining during that search.

Separating the search space reduces the need to train very different student sizes within one shared model. Task-agnostic training also allows selected students to be reused for downstream fine-tuning. On GLUE, the authors report outperforming existing distillation and architecture-search methods, with up to a threefold reduction in computational cost and negligible loss in task performance.
neurips-2022-few-shot-task-agnostic-neur.tldr: AutoDistil searches separately trained architecture subspaces to obtain reusable compressed language models at different computational budgets.

paragraphs: Visual assembly manuals encode useful knowledge about which parts to connect and how to organize construction into feasible steps. Yet assembly agents have made limited use of this information. The paper identifies two obstacles: a shortage of realistic three-dimensional objects paired with manuals, and the difficulty of extracting structured instructions from images.

IKEA-Manual addresses these obstacles with a dataset of 102 IKEA objects and their corresponding assembly manuals. Its annotations describe individual assembly parts, assembly plans, segmented manual content, and correspondences between three-dimensional parts and their two-dimensional depictions. These connections make it possible to relate what a manual shows to the physical components involved.

The authors illustrate the dataset’s use in four tasks: generating assembly plans, segmenting parts, estimating poses, and assembling three-dimensional parts. These applications cover both interpreting instructions and reasoning about object construction. The contribution is a structured resource that brings visual manuals into assembly research, allowing methods to study intermediate construction steps as well as the relationship between drawings and three-dimensional geometry.
neurips-2022-ikea-manual-seeing-shape-as.tldr: IKEA-Manual pairs 102 three-dimensional objects with annotated assembly manuals to support learning assembly from visual instructions.

paragraphs: Modular machine-learning architectures are motivated partly by the idea that real-world processes contain sparsely connected components. A model with similar structure might learn and generalize more effectively. Assessing that intuition is difficult when the true process generating the data is complex and unknown.

This paper studies common modular architectures on simple data distributions whose modular structure is known. That controlled setting makes it possible to examine whether the models obtain the benefits their design is intended to offer. The authors assess both modularity and sparsity, while examining challenges that arise when optimizing systems made of separate interacting components.

The work introduces evaluation metrics that expose where modularity helps and the regimes in which its benefits are substantial. It also finds that current modular systems trained end to end can fall short of their potential. The central implication is that choosing a modular architecture and successfully learning to use its structure are distinct achievements. Known data-generating structure provides a way to measure that gap.
neurips-2022-is-a-modular-architecture-e.tldr: Controlled evaluations show benefits from modularity and sparsity, alongside a gap between modular architectures’ potential and what end-to-end training achieves.

paragraphs: A model that fits noisy training labels perfectly may reproduce that noise on unseen examples. The paper studies this behavior through conditional sampling: the model acts like a sampler from the noisy label distribution associated with an input. Such a model can be a poor classifier when judged by its individual predictions.

The authors develop a learning-theoretic framework for conditional samplers and connect it to knowledge distillation. In distillation, a student learns from a teacher’s outputs on unlabeled examples. They prove that distilling from samplers can produce a student that approximates the Bayes-optimal classifier, the best classification rule for the underlying distribution.

The result distinguishes a teacher’s classification quality from the usefulness of the information it supplies during learning. A noisy teacher can still provide a valuable training signal when it has the sampler behavior analyzed by the framework. The authors also show that familiar methods, including nearest-neighbor algorithms and kernel machines, can often generate such samplers in overparameterized settings.
neurips-2022-knowledge-distillation-bad-.tldr: Models that sample noisy labels can be poor classifiers yet useful teachers, with distillation guarantees under the paper’s sampler framework.

paragraphs: A robot searching for multiple objects must decide how to move and how to gather visual information. With a fixed camera, its limited view can make exploration slow. This paper treats camera movement as a decision-making problem in its own right, aiming to improve navigation by actively looking around.

The authors formulate camera control as a Markov decision process and learn a camera policy with reinforcement learning. A specially designed reward encourages the robot to reveal more of its surroundings through camera movement. A rule-based camera action derived from human experience also guides learning, helping address the difficulty of discovering useful viewing behavior in complex environments.

To coordinate perception with movement, the camera policy considers the navigation policy’s actions when choosing where to look. This links visual exploration to what the robot is doing rather than learning the two decisions in isolation. Experiments show consistent improvements in multi-object navigation over four baselines on two datasets. The findings support active camera control as a useful component of the evaluated navigation systems.
neurips-2022-learning-active-camera-for-.tldr: A learned camera policy coordinated with navigation improves multi-object search by actively gathering useful views.

paragraphs: Multi-task models face two linked problems: tasks can interfere during training, and executing one task can still activate nearly the entire network. M³ViT addresses both by designing the model and its hardware execution together for resource-constrained systems that switch between tasks.

The model incorporates mixture-of-experts layers into a vision transformer. During training, tasks activate sparse sets of specialized experts, separating their parameter usage to avoid training conflicts. At inference, the requested task uses its corresponding sparse pathway. A hardware computation-reordering scheme supports memory-constrained execution, with reported zero-overhead task switching and scalability to any number of experts.

Experiments evaluate software and hardware behavior on PASCAL-Context and NYUD-v2. For single-task inference, the authors report higher accuracy than encoder-focused multi-task methods while reducing inference FLOPs by 88%. On a Xilinx ZCU104 FPGA, the co-design reduces memory requirements by a factor of 2.40 and improves energy efficiency by up to 9.23 times against a comparable FPGA baseline. These findings connect selective model activation with measured deployment benefits.
neurips-2022-m3vit-mixture-of-experts-vi.tldr: M³ViT combines sparse task-specific experts with hardware-aware execution to improve multi-task training and reduce single-task inference costs.

paragraphs: Audio-MAE adapts masked autoencoding from images to audio spectrograms, which organize sound information across time and frequency. The self-supervised learning task is to reconstruct a spectrogram after hiding many of its patches. This lets the model learn representations from the structure of audio itself.

A Transformer encoder processes only the visible patches, using a high masking ratio during this stage. The decoder restores their ordering, inserts tokens for the missing patches, and reconstructs the input. The authors find that local-window attention improves the decoder, matching the strong relationships among nearby time and frequency regions in spectrograms.

For downstream classification, the encoder is fine-tuned using a lower masking ratio. Audio-MAE achieves reported state-of-the-art results on six audio and speech classification tasks, outperforming recent models that use external supervised pretraining. These empirical findings show that masked spectrogram reconstruction can produce useful audio representations. They also identify a concrete adaptation to audio’s local structure within an otherwise straightforward extension of the image-based method.
neurips-2022-masked-autoencoders-that-li.tldr: Audio-MAE learns audio representations by reconstructing heavily masked spectrograms, achieving strong results across six classification tasks.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization is useful when evaluating a candidate solution is expensive and the objective behaves like a black box. Its difficulty grows when a solution has many adjustable variables. This paper tackles that high-dimensional search problem by repeatedly choosing a smaller set of variables to optimize.

MCTS-VS uses Monte Carlo tree search to construct a low-dimensional subspace through variable selection. A Bayesian optimizer then searches within that subspace, and the process iteratively selects and optimizes subsets. The framework can work with any Bayesian optimization algorithm, separating the choice of variables from the optimizer used to explore them.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis of general variable selection to explain how this strategy can work. Experiments include high-dimensional synthetic objectives and real-world problems such as MuJoCo locomotion tasks. They show that MCTS-VS can reach state-of-the-art performance when paired with a suitable Bayesian optimizer. The qualification matters: compatibility with many optimizers does not imply that every pairing achieves the same performance.
neurips-2022-monte-carlo-tree-search-bas.tldr: MCTS-VS uses tree search to select smaller variable subsets, enabling effective high-dimensional Bayesian optimization with a suitable optimizer.

paragraphs: In online learning with feedback graphs, the graph describes which observations become available after a decision. This paper seeks algorithms that perform well in both adversarial environments and stochastic environments. The aim is to retain strong worst-case protection while obtaining smaller regret when the environment has stochastic structure.

The authors develop separate algorithms for strongly and weakly observable directed graphs. For strongly observable graphs, adversarial regret scales roughly with the square root of the independence number times the number of rounds. For weakly observable graphs, it scales with the cube root of a relevant domination number and the two-thirds power of the number of rounds. These rates are nearly tight.

Both algorithms also achieve regret that grows only polylogarithmically with time in stochastic environments. The strongly observable result additionally specifies dependence on the minimum gap between optimal and suboptimal choices and resolves a stated open question. The methods combine follow-the-regularized-leader with new learning-rate updates, providing adaptive guarantees that reflect both the feedback structure and the environment.
neurips-2022-nearly-optimal-best-of-both.tldr: New feedback-graph learning algorithms combine nearly optimal adversarial regret with polylogarithmic stochastic regret.

paragraphs: A sufficient explanation for a decision-tree prediction fixes a subset of an example’s features that guarantees the same prediction for every compatible input. Probabilistic explanations relax that requirement: a random compatible input need only receive the same prediction with probability at least a chosen threshold.

The paper determines the computational difficulty of finding compact explanations of this kind. It distinguishes minimum-size explanations from inclusion-wise minimal ones, where no feature can be removed while preserving the required guarantee. In the general probabilistic problem, neither form admits a polynomial-time algorithm unless P equals NP. Thus, relaxing certainty does not automatically make explanation generation easier.

This contrasts with the deterministic case, where inclusion-wise minimal sufficient explanations are easy to compute. The hardness results settle two open problems and establish difficulty even for decision trees, despite their reputation for interpretability. The authors also identify structural restrictions that make the problem tractable and explain how SAT solvers might address practical instances. Those positive directions distinguish general worst-case hardness from the possibilities available for particular tree structures or solver-based approaches.
neurips-2022-on-computing-probabilistic-.tldr: Finding minimal probabilistic explanations for decision trees is generally computationally hard, although restricted structures admit tractable solutions.

paragraphs: Brain-tumor surgery benefits from accurate diagnosis during the operation, but standard diagnostic workflows require substantial time, labor, and resources. This paper proposes combining stimulated Raman histology, a rapid optical imaging method, with automated image interpretation. Its central contribution is a public dataset supporting research toward that workflow.

OpenSRH includes images from more than 300 brain-tumor patients and over 1,300 distinct whole-slide optical images. It covers common brain-tumor diagnoses and provides pathology annotations, tumor segmentations, and raw and processed imaging data. These materials support developing and validating models across the imaging-to-prediction process.

The authors also provide a framework for classifying whole slides through image patches using patient-level diagnostic labels. They benchmark multiclass tumor classification and patch-based contrastive representation learning. Together, the dataset and framework make the proposed automated interpretation workflow available for systematic study. Improved surgical access, safety, and effectiveness are stated goals for eventual clinical translation; the abstract presents research infrastructure and benchmarks rather than evidence that those clinical outcomes have already improved.
neurips-2022-opensrh-optimizing-brain-tu.tldr: OpenSRH provides annotated brain-tumor optical images and learning benchmarks to support research on rapid diagnosis during surgery.

paragraphs: Information-directed sampling chooses actions using a tradeoff between learning and performance. This paper develops theoretical tools for understanding that tradeoff in reinforcement learning. A central question is what the algorithm should try to learn: the entire environment or a simpler target containing less information.

The authors bound an information ratio and the cumulative information gained about the chosen target. For tabular, finite-horizon Markov decision processes, this yields prior-free Bayesian regret bounds for vanilla IDS that learns the whole environment. They also introduce regularized IDS, replacing a ratio-based objective with an additive one. This computationally efficient variant retains the same regret bound.

Using rate-distortion theory, the authors improve the bound by learning a less informative surrogate environment. This shows how choosing the learning target can affect both computational demands and theoretical performance guarantees. The analysis also extends to linear Markov decision processes and yields related regret bounds for Thompson sampling. The contribution is a broader theoretical account of information-directed exploration and the value of selecting what information to acquire.
neurips-2022-regret-bounds-for-informati.tldr: New regret analyses show how information-directed reinforcement learning can benefit from simpler objectives and carefully chosen learning targets.

paragraphs: Continual-learning models can become biased toward recently seen data and lose performance on earlier tasks. Replay methods counter this by retaining a small collection of historical examples. Retrospective Adversarial Replay, or RAR, aims to make those stored examples more useful by generating challenging variations near the boundary where forgetting occurs.

For a buffered example, RAR finds its nearest neighbor from the current task in a learned representation space and perturbs the stored example toward it. Replaying these samples helps refine the boundary between earlier and current tasks. The framework also uses a MixUp-based strategy that replays mixed augmentations, increasing variation when the historical buffer is small.

The two components address complementary aspects of limited replay: where to place challenging samples and how to diversify them. Experiments report stronger performance than other continual-learning baselines on widely used benchmarks, especially with small buffers. Component ablations and hyperparameter-sensitivity analyses further support the method’s effectiveness and robustness in the evaluated settings. The stated outcome is reduced forgetting, rather than a guarantee that forgetting disappears.
neurips-2022-retrospective-adversarial-r.tldr: RAR reduces continual-learning forgetting by replaying adversarial variations of stored examples together with mixed augmentations.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much interaction with a domain expert can accelerate learning an unknown concept. It studies the learning curve: how prediction error falls as an algorithm receives more examples or asks more questions. The issue is whether interaction changes the rate of improvement.

Earlier uniform bounds describe an upper envelope across families of data distributions. The authors instead use universal learning, which studies behavior on every distribution without demanding one common bound for all of them. This distribution-dependent viewpoint allows a more detailed characterization of learning rates than a single shared worst-case envelope provides.

The main result establishes a three-way classification of universal interactive learning rates, giving a complete characterization in the studied framework. A consequence is an affirmative answer about the benefit of interaction. In important cases, asking for labels through active learning is enough to realize those benefits. Conversely, the lower bounds cover arbitrary binary queries, so allowing more general yes-or-no interaction does not escape the fundamental limits identified by the analysis.
neurips-2022-universal-rates-for-interac.tldr: A distribution-dependent theory classifies interactive learning rates and shows when expert interaction, including label queries, accelerates learning.

paragraphs: Unpaired image translation learns to change an image’s domain while preserving important semantic content, without matched examples of the desired transformation. The paper emphasizes that such data cannot determine an optimal mapping without assumptions. Its proposed assumption concerns how probable local image patches are in their respective domains.

Specifically, patches from high-density regions of one domain should map to high-density regions of the other. The authors train flow models to estimate these patch densities and penalize variation in density changes during translation. This provides an efficient regularization mechanism that makes the statistical assumption part of the training objective.

The method reports the best performance on the evaluated benchmark datasets while requiring only 56–86% of the training time of the existing state-of-the-art method. These findings suggest that a relatively simple density-based constraint can improve both translation performance and training efficiency in those settings. The approach’s rationale depends on the stated correspondence between high-density patches across domains; its benchmark success supplies empirical support for using that assumption.
neurips-2022-unsupervised-image-to-image.tldr: A patch-density consistency assumption yields an efficient regularizer that improves unpaired image translation on the evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Large pretrained models can sometimes be fine-tuned privately with performance close to non-private models, despite theoretical concerns about growing model size. This paper investigates when high dimensionality need not worsen the privacy–utility tradeoff. Its focus is the size of gradients after projection onto different subspaces.

For convex learning, the authors introduce restricted Lipschitz continuity to describe the relevant structure of the objective. They derive improved bounds on excess empirical and population risk that become independent of dimension under additional conditions. The result identifies circumstances in which parameter count alone does not determine the theoretical cost of private learning.

The empirical analysis examines gradients during private fine-tuning of large language models. These gradients are mostly controlled by a few principal components, resembling the structure associated with the convex theory’s dimension-independent guarantees. This provides a possible explanation for successful large-scale private fine-tuning. The connection is suggestive rather than a proof that the convex guarantees directly apply to language-model training.
neurips-2022-when-does-differentially-pr.tldr: Structured gradients can yield dimension-independent private-learning bounds under conditions and may help explain successful private language-model fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Human moral judgments often follow rules while allowing exceptions in unusual circumstances. Predicting those exceptions is a challenge for systems intended to understand human decisions. This paper introduces MoralExceptQA, a question-answering challenge set inspired by moral psychology and focused on situations involving potentially permissible exceptions.

The authors also propose MoralCoT, a prompting strategy that combines a large language model with theories of moral reasoning from cognitive science. Its purpose is to predict human judgments by incorporating reasoning about moral exceptions into the prompting process. The dataset and method therefore address both how to evaluate this flexibility and how to encourage it in a model.

MoralCoT outperforms seven existing language models by a reported 6.2% F1. The authors interpret this as suggesting that modeling human reasoning might be necessary to capture moral flexibility; the result does not establish that necessity. A detailed error analysis identifies directions for further work. The study concerns predicting human moral judgments, so the measured improvement should be understood as better agreement on that task.
neurips-2022-when-to-make-exceptions-exp.tldr: MoralExceptQA and MoralCoT study moral exceptions, with cognitively informed prompting improving prediction of human judgments.
